extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers, humorists, and fans interested in David Sedaris' MasterClass
extracted.subtask_description: Summary and highlights of David Sedaris's MasterClass on storytelling and humor, emphasizing his practical writing habits and craft lessons (diary-keeping, daily writing, heavy revision, observation, connecting with readers, and performing). Useful for writers studying craft or considering the course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be interested in people
rubrics_metrics.description: "If you write about people, you have to be interested in people."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sedaris frames interest in people as foundational: ask unexpected, specific questions to generate material and observe human behavior. This is a criterion for subject selection and empathetic attention rather than plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use unexpected, concrete questions as prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask surprising questions like “Do your children shower?” or “Who’s the drunkest customer you’ve had today?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These kinds of pointed, odd questions are presented as generators of unique detail and anecdote; they encourage writers to notice and record the small, revealing facts that make stories distinctive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a diary
rubrics_metrics.description: "Keep a diary in which to record the answers, and with which, even more importantly, to maintain a daily writing habit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The diary functions both as an archive of observations and as the engine of routine practice. Sedaris emphasizes using it to capture material and to sustain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a daily writing habit
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris "writes every day without fail" and recommends daily writing practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daily writing is presented as non-negotiable for craft development; Sedaris contrasts habitual daily work with writing "when it strikes me," implying the latter is weaker for consistent improvement and output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist long-term before expecting success
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris wrote every day for fifteen years before "The Santaland Diaries" brought attention and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets an expectation of long-term persistence: years of steady practice and accumulation of material may precede recognition. It's an encouragement to value process over immediate payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise extensively (do many rewrites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris does "twelve to eighteen rewrites of each piece."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavy revision is treated as essential to crafting a strong piece. The numeric range gives explicit expectation for thorough rewriting rather than minimal edits; suggests iterative tightening and polishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the world
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the course topics is "observing the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active observation—noticing details, behaviors, and oddities—is a skill to cultivate. Observation supplies the raw materials (details, scenes, lines) that fuel essays and stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hear and attend to craft (attention to construction and words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris criticizes listeners who don't "pay attention to how [a piece] is constructed" or the words used; he urges students to "hear the craft of it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should focus on sentence-level choices, narrative construction, and phrasing. The ability to detect craft in others' work is presented as a teachable, desirable skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect with the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: One lesson covers "connecting with the reader."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies choices in tone, detail, pacing, and empathy that invite readers into the piece. Guidance includes using concrete detail and honest voice to build trust and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with weight
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings should carry emotional or thematic payoff; they should feel earned and give the reader a sense of closure or resonance. This is an editorial criterion for structural and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write about loved ones thoughtfully (consider their perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lesson titled "writing about loved ones" includes Sedaris's sister Lisa speaking about what it feels like to be written about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using family as material, consider ethical implications and the subjects' perspectives; include voices of those depicted (as Sedaris does with his sister) to acknowledge effects on real people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for readings and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris gives readings of diary entries and published pieces and offers advice on how to handle readings of one's own in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance and oral presentation are part of the craft for many humorists: practicing aloud, shaping pieces for voice, and learning stage presence are evaluative dimensions for public delivery of work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry a notebook and capture ideas on the go
rubrics_metrics.description: Related guidance (cited in linked material) includes "carry a notebook" as part of Sedaris's process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical habit: keep a place to record sudden observations or lines. This complements diary-keeping and ensures fleeting details aren't lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read your work out loud
rubrics_metrics.description: Related guidance includes "read out loud" as part of Sedaris's process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud is recommended to catch rhythm, awkward phrasing, and comedic timing; it's also tied to preparing pieces for live readings and radio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value craft over instant likability
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedaris notes that popular pieces (e.g., "Santaland Diaries") may be "clunkily written," and that many listeners miss the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion here is to prioritize careful construction and word choice even if a piece's popularity masks its flaws; cultivating craft is an aim in itself, separate from immediate audience reaction.
